newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia's Lebed ends first visit to West.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed ends first visit to West.

text.p: Russian security tsar Alexander Lebed ended his first visit to the West on Wednesday having impressed his hosts with a "down-to-earth" style which avoided open brawling over NATO's plans to expand eastwards.

Lebed flew out of Brussels shortly after midday, formally closing a trip which many saw as confirming him in the role of "president in waiting" should the ailing Boris Yeltsin fail to recover from heart problems.
"Our feeling was that here we had a man with whom you could negotiate," one NATO official said.
Lebed spent two days touring the alliance's sprawling political headquarters in Brussels and its military nerve centre at Mons in southern Belgium.
He studiously avoided any repetition of previous anti-NATO outbursts -- his gravelly voice instead delivering a statesman-like mixture of encouragements and chidings to his former Cold War foe.

At meetings with the world's media, a smiling Lebed praised NATO's efficiency, pledged more Russian cooperation, and -- crucially -- said it had the right to expand although he would prefer it not to do so, and certainly not so soon.
"It was a persuasive argument and one which could create difficulties for NATO," one alliance source said.

NATO sources said Lebed, a reserve paratroop general clearly at ease in the military world, had expressed an interest in becoming more involved in the "enlargement dossier" -- until now the sole preserve of the foreign ministry.
"If that happens we may have a real interlocutor at long last, he has a refreshingly new style, but it is a very big if," added the official.
Lebed, who was criticised by his many opponents while out of Moscow, could be heading back to more trouble.

On Wednesday, Russian news agencies reported he had been summoned to appear before parliament -- dominated by old communist hardliners -- to clarify his position on NATO following his talks in Brussels.
NATO has said it plans to name countries next year with which it intends to open membership talks with Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic leading the field.
Lebed clearly relished his debut on the world political stage.
He emerged from NATO's military command on Tuesday and described what he had seen as an "efficient, well-tuned military machine".
Lebed earlier inspected an honour guard of allied soldiers with Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. General George Joulwan, before touring SHAPE headquarters.
The sprawling military headquarters would have played a major part in directing any military operations against the now disbanded Warsaw Pact which Lebed served through most of his career.
"We spoke as two soldiers," Lebed said after emerging into the sunshine from the central control building known as Live Oak. "We talked as two paratroopers."
